lab_title: VSEPR Theory: Predicting 3D Molecular Geometry from Lewis Structures
top_level_objectives: Use Lewis structures to count electron domains around a central atom and distinguish bonding pairs from lone pairs.
Predict the five fundamental electron-domain geometries using the VSEPR principle of minimizing electron-pair repulsions.
Identify common molecular geometries produced when lone pairs occupy positions in electron-domain arrangements.
Explain why lone pairs compress bond angles relative to ideal geometries and compare predictions with real molecular examples.

scenes.scene_name: From Lewis Structure to Electron Domains
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the workflow from a 2D Lewis structure to the number and type of electron domains around a central atom.
key_visuals: A flat Lewis structure panel with examples such as CH4, NH3, and H2O
A highlighted central atom with bonding domains and lone-pair domains color-coded
A simple counter showing total electron domains versus bonding domains
student_actions: Select the central atom in each Lewis structure.
Tap bonds and lone pairs to classify them as electron domains.
Confirm the electron-domain count before moving to 3D prediction.

scenes.brief_purpose: Show that electron domains arrange in three dimensions to maximize separation and minimize repulsion.
key_visuals: A central atom surrounded by movable electron-domain clouds
Repulsion arrows between domains that shrink as spacing improves
A before-and-after view showing domains settling into a stable arrangement
student_actions: Drag electron domains around the central atom and observe repulsion indicators.
Release the domains to let the model settle into the lowest-repulsion geometry.
Explain in a short prompt why evenly spaced domains are favored.

scenes.brief_purpose: Build the fundamental VSEPR electron-domain geometries for 2 through 6 domains.
key_visuals: Side-by-side 3D models of linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral arrangements
A rotating central atom model for each domain count
student_actions: Choose a domain count from 2 to 6 and predict the electron-domain geometry.
Rotate each model to view the arrangement in 3D.
Match each geometry name to its domain count and ideal bond angles.

scenes.scene_name: Molecular Geometry When Lone Pairs Are Present
scenes.brief_purpose: Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry by hiding lone pairs from the named molecular shape.
key_visuals: Tetrahedral electron-domain models transforming into trigonal pyramidal and bent molecular shapes
Trigonal bipyramidal models showing seesaw and T-shaped outcomes
Octahedral models showing square pyramidal and square planar outcomes
student_actions: Replace one or more bonding domains with lone pairs in a selected electron-domain geometry.
Observe how the visible atom positions define the molecular geometry.
Label the resulting shape from a menu of common VSEPR shapes.

scenes.brief_purpose: Explain why lone pairs take up more angular space and compress adjacent bond angles.
key_visuals: Methane and water models shown side by side
Ideal tetrahedral angle label of 109.5° contrasted with water’s 104.5° H–O–H angle
Lone-pair electron clouds drawn larger than bonding-pair clouds with stronger repulsion indicators
student_actions: Compare bond angles in CH4, NH3, and H2O.
Toggle lone-pair repulsion strength to see bond angles compress.
Answer a brief check explaining why water is bent and has a smaller angle than methane.

scenes.brief_purpose: Apply the full VSEPR workflow to common molecules and compare predictions with observed structures.
key_visuals: Interactive molecule cards for H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, and XeF4
Student-built VSEPR models next to observed 3D molecular structures
Feedback highlights showing correct domain count, electron geometry, molecular geometry, and approximate bond angles
student_actions: For each molecule, count electron domains from the Lewis structure.
Predict electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry.
Compare the prediction to the observed model and revise any incorrect classifications.
